clinicalPearls: Mesomelic (middle-segment) limb shortening with disproportionate short stature is the core feature.
Madelung deformity of the wrist is the clinical hallmark: bowing of the radius, dorsal prominence of the distal ulna and volar-ulnar tilt of the carpus.
Caused by SHOX (short-stature homeobox) haploinsufficiency — deletions or mutations of SHOX or its regulatory enhancers in the pseudoautosomal region (PAR1).
SHOX escapes X-inactivation and is present on both the X and Y chromosomes, which is why its loss underlies the short stature of Turner syndrome.
The phenotype is typically more marked in females, attributed to oestrogen effects on the growth plate.
Biallelic (homozygous or compound-heterozygous) SHOX loss causes the severe Langer mesomelic dysplasia, whereas Léri-Weill is the milder heterozygous form.
An increased carrying angle, an apparent muscular build, and forearm and wrist symptoms are commonly seen.
Early recognition guides growth-promoting therapy considerations, orthopaedic planning and genetic counselling.
reference.pathophysiology: Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis results from haploinsufficiency of SHOX, the short-stature homeobox-containing gene located in pseudoautosomal region 1 (PAR1) at the tips of the short arms of the X and Y chromosomes. SHOX encodes a transcription factor important for the proliferation and orderly differentiation of growth-plate chondrocytes. Most cases arise from whole-gene deletions, from deletions of upstream or downstream enhancer elements, or from point mutations that reduce functional gene dosage. Because SHOX escapes X-inactivation and is normally expressed from both sex chromosomes, loss of a single functional copy lowers gene dosage sufficiently to disturb endochondral growth, producing mesomelic limb shortening and the Madelung deformity of the wrist. The greater severity in females is attributed to the influence of oestrogen on the growth plate. Homozygous or compound-heterozygous loss of SHOX produces the far more severe Langer mesomelic dysplasia, while heterozygous loss also underlies a proportion of idiopathic short stature and contributes to the short stature of Turner syndrome, in which monosomy X leaves only a single SHOX copy. Inheritance is described as pseudoautosomal dominant.
additionalDifferentials: Langer mesomelic dysplasia (biallelic SHOX loss) — the severe end of the same spectrum
Turner syndrome (45,X) — SHOX haploinsufficiency plus additional systemic features
Other mesomelic dysplasias, e.g., Robinow syndrome (ROR2/WNT5A), Nievergelt and Kozlowski types
Hereditary multiple exostoses causing forearm deformity and a pseudo-Madelung appearance
Post-traumatic or infective growth-plate injury producing an acquired Madelung-like deformity
Idiopathic short stature, a proportion of which is SHOX-related
additionalInvestigations: Wrist and forearm radiographs for Madelung deformity (radial bowing, pyramidalisation of the carpus, dorsal ulnar subluxation)
Anthropometry with segment ratios (arm span and sitting height) to document mesomelia
SHOX molecular analysis: deletion/duplication testing (MLPA or array) including enhancers, plus sequencing for point mutations
Karyotype or genomic array to exclude Turner syndrome in girls with short stature
Skeletal survey to characterise the disproportion and exclude mimics
Serial growth-chart plotting and bone-age assessment
Endocrine and growth assessment to inform consideration of growth-promoting therapy
redFlags: Progressive wrist pain, deformity or restricted movement from an advancing Madelung deformity
Marked disproportion or severe short stature suggesting biallelic (Langer) disease
Features suggesting Turner syndrome, which mandate a karyotype and carry cardiac, renal and gonadal implications
reference.prognosis: Stature is reduced but intellect and life expectancy are normal. The main morbidity is wrist dysfunction and cosmetic deformity from the Madelung deformity, which may require orthopaedic intervention. Early diagnosis allows growth, orthopaedic and reproductive counselling to be planned.
pitfalls: Overlooking Turner syndrome in a short girl with a SHOX-type phenotype — always consider a karyotype
Relying on sequencing alone and missing SHOX or enhancer deletions, which require deletion/duplication analysis
Attributing the Madelung deformity solely to trauma or to exostoses
Underestimating the female predominance and severity, delaying diagnosis in girls
Forgetting the pseudoautosomal (not purely X-linked) inheritance when counselling families
references: Nosology and classification of genetic skeletal disorders
Paediatric endocrinology and growth reference texts
management: Recombinant growth hormone therapy to improve stature, as used for SHOX deficiency
Orthopaedic management of the Madelung deformity, including corrective radial osteotomy and Vickers ligament release where symptomatic
Wrist splinting, physiotherapy and analgesia for wrist pain and dysfunction
Serial monitoring of growth, skeletal proportions and bone age to guide timing of intervention
Paediatric endocrinology and orthopaedic multidisciplinary care
Genetic counselling and family screening given SHOX haploinsufficiency in the pseudoautosomal region
Reproductive counselling regarding transmission risk and the more severe biallelic Langer mesomelic dysplasia
